passages.happening:
“You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense” (verse 1). It is small and square, a cubit by a cubit and two cubits high, with horns, covered with pure gold, with rings and poles (verses 2-5). It stands in front of the veil, before the mercy seat, “where I will meet with you” (verse 6).

“And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps” (verse 7), and again at twilight, “perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come” (verse 8). No other incense and no other offering may be put on it (verse 9). “Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Moses is still on the mountain. Chapter 29 reached its high point in God's promise to dwell among his people. Chapter 30 turns to what will keep the sanctuary working day after day: incense morning and evening, washing before every approach, a ransom for every life, and an oil that marks things and people as God's.

And the reader knows what Moses does not yet know. At the foot of the mountain the people are about to make a golden calf.

This second altar is small and golden, and it stands inside the tent, just in front of the veil. Twice a day, as the lamps are tended, incense rises from it before God.

Why is it described here and not in chapter 25 with the other furniture? Many critical scholars think chapters 30 and 31 were added later. Others answer that chapter 25 describes the furniture of God's house, and chapter 30 gathers the things that belong to the priests' daily service.

Small stone altars with horns have been found at several sites in Israel, among them Megiddo and the shrine at Arad. The shape was a familiar one.

No unauthorized incense may be burned on it. Only what God commanded may be offered here.
passages.later:
On the Day of Atonement the high priest took incense behind the veil, “and the cloud of incense will cover the mercy seat above the Testimony, so that he will not die” (Leviticus 16:13).

When King Uzziah grew proud, “he entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense” (2 Chronicles 26:16), a work only priests could do, and he was struck with a skin disease.

A psalm makes incense a picture of prayer: “May my prayer be set before You like incense” (Psalm 141:2). Zechariah was serving at this altar when an angel “appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense” (Luke 1:11). And in Revelation, incense rises “together with the prayers of the saints” before God (Revelation 8:4).
passages.asks: Incense rose before God every morning and every evening. Ask what rises from your life to God at the start and the end of each day. And ask whether you come to God on his terms, or offer him what you have chosen for yourself.

passages.happening:
“When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered” (verse 12).

Each one pays half a shekel (verse 13), everyone twenty years old or more (verse 14). “the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less” (verse 15). The money is for the service of the Tent of Meeting, “a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD to make atonement for your lives” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Coins did not yet exist. Silver was weighed out, and the shekel was a weight, roughly 11 to 12 grams. Half a shekel was a small but real amount.

A census was not neutral bookkeeping in that world. It was taken to muster men for war or to tax them, and twenty was the age of military service. To count people was to claim them. But Israel's people belonged to God, who had redeemed them from Egypt. The ransom was a confession that every counted life was his.

Rich and poor pay exactly the same. Before God every life is worth the same ransom.

Later the census silver was melted down to make the silver bases that held up the frames of the tabernacle. The house of God stood, quite literally, on the redemption money of the whole people. In later times the half shekel became a yearly tax for the temple.
passages.later:
When the silver was gathered, it came to “a beka per person, that is, half a shekel” (Exodus 38:26), and “The hundred talents of silver were used to cast the bases of the sanctuary” (Exodus 38:27).

David's census was followed by a plague, and David confessed, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done” (2 Samuel 24:10).

The temple tax collectors asked Peter, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” (Matthew 17:24). Peter writes that believers were redeemed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” (1 Peter 1:18), “but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).
passages.hard:
Why would counting the people bring a plague?

The Bible does not treat counting as wrong in itself. The book of Numbers is named for two censuses God commands. The danger lies in who owns what is counted. A census served war and taxes, and a ruler who counts his people is claiming them as his own resources. Israel's people belong to God, and the ransom confesses that their lives are his. Interpreters differ on how much an older fear of counting, found in the ancient world, lies in the background, but the chapter's own reasoning is clear.
passages.asks: Rich and poor paid the same ransom. Ask whether you treat some people as worth more than others because of what they have. And ask whose you believe your life is: your own, your employer's, your country's, or God's.

passages.happening:
“You are to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it, with which Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet” (verses 18-19).

“Whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister by presenting an offering made by fire to the LORD, they must wash with water so that they will not die” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The basin stood in the courtyard, between the altar and the tent. Every time the priests went in to serve, they washed their hands and feet.

The priests had been washed once, at their ordination (29:4). Now they wash again and again. Holy service requires a cleanness that is renewed, not taken for granted.

The warning comes back: ‘so that they will not die’. Coming near a holy God is not a small thing.
passages.later:
A psalm asks who may come into God's presence: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:4).

Hebrews urges believers to draw near to God, “having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22).
passages.asks: The priests washed every time they came to serve. Ask whether you come to God carrying things you have not confessed. And ask what it means that cleansing is offered again and again, not only once.

passages.happening:
“Take the finest spices: 500 shekels of liquid myrrh, half that amount (250 shekels) of fragrant cinnamon, 250 shekels of fragrant cane, 500 shekels of cassia” (verses 23-24), with olive oil. “Prepare from these a sacred anointing oil” (verse 25).

With it Moses is to anoint the tent and everything in it (verses 26-28). “You are to consecrate them so that they will be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy” (verse 29). “Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests” (verse 30).

“It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man, and you must not make anything like it with the same formula. It is holy, and it must be holy to you” (verse 32). Anyone who copies it or puts it on an outsider “shall be cut off from his people” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The spices came from far away. Myrrh is a tree resin from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, carried north by caravan. Cinnamon and cassia most likely came from farther east. The identity of some ingredients, such as the fragrant cane, is uncertain.

Anointing with oil was how kings and priests were put into office. The oil marked a person or thing as set apart. Everything in the tabernacle was anointed with it, and so were the priests.

That is why the recipe was protected. If anyone could make this oil for pleasure, the sign that marked God's house and his priests would become one more luxury.

‘Cut off from his people’ is a phrase whose meaning is debated. Some take it as death at the hands of the community. Others take it as a punishment God himself carries out, such as early death or the loss of descendants. Others take it as being put out of Israel.
passages.later:
A psalm pictures unity as this oil: “It is like fine oil on the head, running down on the beard, running down Aaron’s beard over the collar of his robes” (Psalm 133:2).

Jesus read Isaiah in the synagogue and applied it to himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me” (Luke 4:18). The title Messiah means the Anointed One.
passages.asks: God kept some things for himself alone. Ask whether you treat holy things, prayer, worship, the Lord's Supper, as ordinary. And ask what in your life is set apart for God and not for your own use.

passages.happening:
God names four fragrant spices, gum resin, onycha, galbanum and pure frankincense, “in equal measures” (verse 34). They are made into “a fragrant blend of incense, the work of a perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy” (verse 35).

“Grind some of it into fine powder and place it in front of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you” (verse 36).

“You are never to use this formula to make incense for yourselves; you shall regard it as holy to the LORD” (verse 37). Anyone who makes it to enjoy its smell will be cut off (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Incense filled the temples and palaces of the ancient world. It honored a god or a king and sweetened the air. Frankincense, like myrrh, is a tree resin from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa. The exact identity of onycha is uncertain.

The incense is placed ‘in front of the Testimony’, as near the ark as anything in the chapter. The chapter moves from the inner room outward and back again: the altar before the veil, silver for the tent, the basin in the court, oil for everything, and last, incense before the ark.

As with the oil, the recipe belongs to God. It is not for perfume at home.

Chapters 25 to 31 are built from seven speeches of God to Moses, each opened by ‘the LORD said to Moses’. This chapter holds four of them. The seventh, in chapter 31, is about the Sabbath. Many readers see an echo of the seven days of creation: the God who made a world now builds a small world to live in.
passages.later:
Revelation shows an angel at “the golden altar before the throne”, given “much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints” (Revelation 8:3).

Paul writes, “For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:15).
passages.asks: The incense was holy because it was offered to God, not used for pleasure. Ask whether your prayers are offered to God or performed for others. And ask what it would mean for your life to be, in Paul's words, the sweet aroma of Christ.
